title: Former Boxing Champion Jorge Linares in ICE Custody, Facing Deportation From US
excerpt: ICE says the Venezuelan three-weight world champion overstayed a temporary stay that began in October 2023; his lawyers say he is authorised to be in the United States.
body:
• Former three-weight world boxing champion Jorge Linares, 41, was arrested by Border Patrol agents and ICE officers at El Paso International Airport on Sunday, November 15, and remains in ICE custody in Texas pending deportation proceedings.
  • ICE says Linares entered the United States on October 26, 2023, with permission for a temporary stay and remained beyond the authorised period; the agency states that a pending application or work authorisation does not confer legal status.
  • His lawyers, Wilner & O'Reilly, say he is authorised to be in the United States, has cooperated fully, and are working with ICE to resolve the matter.
  • No hearing date has been announced; for any non-citizen, the case is a reminder that status disputes are decided in removal proceedings, not at the airport.

Jorge Linares, the Venezuelan former world boxing champion, is in the custody of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Texas and facing deportation, after Border Patrol agents and ICE officers arrested him at El Paso International Airport on Sunday. Linares announced the detention himself on X: “I'm being held by ICE in El Paso, Texas. What a crazy situation,” he wrote, according to CNN.

ICE's account

An ICE spokesperson told CNN that Linares was “a foreign national in the country without legal immigration status, arriving from Venezuela.” According to ICE, he entered the country on October 26, 2023, on a permit for a temporary stay and “remained in the country beyond the authorized period,” and he will remain in custody pending deportation proceedings. In a statement reported by the BBC, an ICE spokesperson added: “To be clear, a pending application or work authorisation does not confer legal status in the United States.”

"On October 26, 2023, he entered the country with permission to stay for a temporary period, but in defiance of our nation's laws, he overstayed his welcome. He will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings."

— ICE spokesperson, via BBC

His lawyers' account

The immigration law firm Wilner & O'Reilly, which represents Linares, disputes ICE's characterisation. “Mr Linares is authorised to be in the United States and he has cooperated fully with immigration authorities,” the firm said in a statement. “We are in communication with ICE and are working to resolve this matter as quickly as possible. Immigration matters follow established procedures, and those procedures take time. We are confident in Mr. Linares's position and ask his fans, the press and the public for patience in the meantime.” Neither side has publicly produced the document on which the dispute turns — the terms of the permission under which Linares entered in October 2023.

Who Linares is

Born in Barinitas, Venezuela, the 41-year-old won 47 of his 56 professional bouts in a career that began in 2002, taking world titles at featherweight, super-featherweight and lightweight. A significant portion of his career was fought in Japan, and he fought more than 10 times in the United States. He retired after losing to Britain's Jack Catterall in a light-welterweight bout in October 2023. He is based in Miami. Gilberto J. Mendoza, president of the World Boxing Association, confirmed the detention on Monday: “I can confirm that my friend Jorge Linares, a former WBA world champion, is in ICE custody,” adding that immigration attorneys were handling the case and that he remained in constant contact with the fighter's family.

What happens next

Linares remains in ICE custody pending removal proceedings, in which an immigration judge — not the arresting officers — will decide whether the government has established that he overstayed, and whether any application he has pending changes that outcome. No hearing date has been announced, and his lawyers have not said whether they will seek his release while the case proceeds. The point of general application in ICE's statement is the one his case now tests in public: under US immigration law, having an application pending, or holding work authorisation, is not the same as holding lawful status — a distinction that decides cases like this one.
